subject: ARCH
title: Top Modules Arch & Praxis
comments: Blind Design Workshop. Undergrads only. Grads use ARCH 5134. In the spring of 2026, a group of learners who are blind or visually-impaired, organized by the Virginia Department for the Blind and Vision Impaired (DBVI), will participate in an immersive design workshop at Virginia Tech which will be led by faculty and students of the Schools of Architecture + Design. The workshop will engage participants with a blind-accessible design project, supplemented by guest lectures, videos + readings, tours of sites in and around the university, and instruction in emerging building technologies. It will provide career exploration experience in the discipline of architecture, and give participants the opportunity to improve their self-advocacy skills while interacting with university students and navigating a college campus. Virginia Tech students, working under the guidance of Dr. Andrew Gipe-Lazarou, will receive university credit for preparing and instructing the workshop, which will both address the spatial needs of the blind community and call into question the ‘ocular-centrism’ of design by exploring ways in which architecture can be instructed non-visually. Workshop preparation will be supplemented by a hands-on tutorial organized by DBVI about working / interacting with individuals who are blind or visually impaired.

subject: ARCH
title: Topics Bldg Science & Tech
comments: Material Design: From Nanoscale Building Blocks to Macroscale Structures. Undergraduates only. Graduates please use ARCH 5116. In this course, we examine the interplay between man-made and natural materials. We will investigate how nano properties influence macro scale applications, with a focus on synthetic, bioinspired, and biomaterials. Students will design, fabricate, and test their own materials, bridging theoretical concepts with practical applications. We will explore both traditional material engineering and bioengineering approaches, assessing how biological principles inform sustainable design. Students will analyze and characterize their creations using cutting-edge methods in material science, such as Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), Nanoindentation, and Universal Testing Machine (UTM). By the end of the course, students will be equipped with a critical, creative mindset for material specification in architectural design and construction. This course is designed to make complex material science accessible, with no prior knowledge required, and will inspire students to explore new possibilities in architecture, from the molecular scale to the building scale Join us as we explore new worlds from nano to macro!"

subject: ARCH
title: Topics Bldg Science & Tech
comments: Energy & Daylight Building Simulation. Undergrads only. Graduates use ARCH 5064. Achieving the optimal design isn't always guaranteed by good intentions alone. Sometimes, relying solely on intuition and general guidelines falls short in making well-informed decisions. This course is designed to introduce students to the use of several advanced building simulation tools, including the COVE tool (Energy Simulation), Grasshopper (Climate Report), and Climate Studio (Daylight simulation). The course will fill the gap between qualitative and quantitative aspects of design, considering the user experience in the daylight simulation stage. The primary focus is on designing and optimizing sustainable building systems through energy modeling in the early design stages to reduce environmental impact and enhance energy efficiency. Students will gain an understanding of the natural forces and human comfort factors that drive sustainable systems, as well as the various systems and cycles of our planet, including energy, atmosphere, and climate. No prior experience is required, and all licenses will be provided.

subject: ARCH
title: Topics Bldg Science & Tech
comments: Building the Future of Construction. Undergrads only, Grads use ARCH 5064. As part of the CDR OpenLab and through this project-based collaboration with the National Building Museum (NBM), the Center for Design Research(CDR) course will envision “the air and space museum for construction” through the development of experiential exhibitions that address cycles of innovation in construction’s past, present, and future and engage stakeholders across disciplines, ages, and backgrounds. During the course students will explore the museum as a place of culture and learning while experimenting with technologies such as XR and spatial computing. Course is open to all disciplines and levels and will include travel to Washington DC for an NBM visit.

subject: ARCH
title: Top Arch Media & Methods
comments: Drawing: Traces of Seeing and Thinking Only for 2nd, 3rd, 4th, and 5th year Architecture Students. “I want to see things. I don’t trust anything else. I place things in front of me on the paper so that I can see them. I want to see therefore I draw.” (C. Scarpa) “Our thoughts are not linear: they leap backwards and forwards, and our drawings have to adapt to this. Drawing should help us think... When multiple options arise, the act of drawing should let us waver. If you draw without erasing anything, you can just keep adding more and more layers…so that the whole process remains visible.” (Flores & Prats) This three credit hour professional elective course will explore historical and emerging approaches to hand sketching and drawing, ranges of representational typologies, digital work and simulation approaches. From a theory perspective, texts ranging from Scheer’s The Death of Drawing to Kahn’s The Importance of A Drawing will be used plus a wide range of other sources. Open to 2nd year through thesis students, as a vertical cohort, students will actively consider both theoretical and practice-based (their own) work. Faculty members from across the School will lead the efforts through lectures, discussions and reviews. Students will create at least three pin-up presentations/exhibitions over the semester that combine students’ design process and application of newly discovered topics and approaches.

subject: ARCH
title: Top Arch Media & Methods
comments: Immersive Design (VR +AI). Undergrads only, Grads use 5064. This course explores the rapidly evolving convergence of artificial intelligence (AI), virtual reality (VR), real-time rendering, and animation in design visualization. Students will gain hands-on experience with industry-leading platforms—Enscape, Twinmotion, and D5—while learning how to integrate AI-driven ideation and creativity tools into their design and storytelling workflows. The course Explores techniques for rendering, animation, and immersive VR experiences. Each platform will be presented not just as a visualization tool, but as a gateway to designing, animating, and experiencing projects in VR. Through these stages, students will explore the intersection of creativity, technical mastery, and narrative design—using AI to amplify imagination, animation to craft compelling stories, and VR to immerse audiences in bold new realities. Whether you’re new to these tools or looking to sharpen your skills, this course is designed to help you unlock your creative potential!

subject: ARCH
title: Top Arch Media & Methods
comments: The Photographic Print: Static, Serial, and Dynamic. Undergrads only, Grads use ARCH 5116. Introduction to black and white photographic printmaking in the darkroom by exploring operations of scale and space, pattern, and the concept of camouflage.

subject: ARCH
title: Top Arch Media & Methods
comments: Architectural BIM (Revit), Undergrads only, Grads use ARCH 5064. This course introduces you to the core concepts and tools of Building Information Modeling (BIM) using Autodesk Revit. You'll gain the skills to create, analyze, and present architectural designs in both technical and visually compelling ways. Each week, we’ll explore key topics in detail, with clear explanations and hands-on exercises to help you really understand the material. As you progress, you’ll have the opportunity to apply your skills in more complex projects, building your confidence and expertise along the way. Whether you’re new to these tools or looking to sharpen your skills, this course is designed to help you unlock your creative potential!

subject: ARCH
title: Top Arch Media & Methods
comments: Check computer requirements before enrolling in this course. Email cpritche@vt.edu for more information. Undergraduates only. Grads please use ARCH 5116. This course introduces architecture students to the capabilities of Unreal Engine 5 for architectural visualization. Students will learn how to create immersive environments, render high-quality images, cinematics, and be introduced to blueprint coding language. Through a blend of technical tutorials and projects, students will explore lighting, materials, and real-time rendering techniques.

subject: ARCH
title: Top Arch Media & Methods
comments: Digital Modeling & Post-pro. Undergrads only, Grads use 5064. This course is an exciting blend of Rhinoceros for conceptual design, and Adobe Photoshop for post-production—giving you a well-rounded skill set to create and enhance stunning digital designs. You’ll start by mastering 2D drafting and progress to designing intricate 3D models using Rhinoceros, building a strong foundation in precision modeling. Then, in the post-production phase, we’ll dive into Photoshop’s advanced effects and visual techniques to polish your visuals with professional flair. Whether you’re new to these tools or looking to sharpen your skills, this course is designed to help you unlock your creative potential!

subject: ARCH
title: Top Arch Media & Methods
comments: Comp Design & Fabrication. Undergrads only, Grads use ARCH 5064. The Integrated Computational Design & Fabrication (ICDF) course introduces students to the intersection of computational design and digital fabrication in architecture. Students will gain hands-on experience with Grasshopper 3D, learning to design free-form objects/structures and create prototypes using advanced digital fabrication tools like Robotic Arm, CNC machines, and 3D printers. Through weekly modeling assignments and group projects, students will design and prototype an installation, integrating computational thinking with practical fabrication techniques. In the last month, we will make one of the projects on a real scale. The course aims to familiarize students with digital tools and processes, highlighting how fabrication capabilities influence architectural design and construction.

subject: ARCH
title: Top Arch Media & Methods
comments: Undergrads only, Grads use ARCH 5115. As an initial response to the limitations on travel during the pandemic, this elective course was developed in 2020 to allow students to engage in travel study through drawing without traveling physically. Using digital means, we “traveled” to 15 locations across the world and worked through a series of drawing exercises that equipped students with the habits and ways of thinking through drawing—to see, study, and analyze their future physical travel experiences as architects. The review of drawings on screen via zoom worked surprisingly well with greater ability to engage with the “tactics” and decision process of making a drawing enabling direct discussion, critique, and demonstration from both the instructor and student colleagues. In Spring of 2026, this course returns as a hybrid course designed to focus your understanding of sketching practices as an architect. Emphasis will be on formulating “the page” as a drawing problem. How do you plan a series of drawings with an intention; making drawings that are exploratory and analytic, working to build pages in a sketchbook that (foster?) an understanding of what you see rather than simply “taking a pic.” Various approaches to drawing are explored and experiment will be encouraged.

subject: ARCH
title: Top Arch & Praxis
comments: Human-Centric Design: The Art and Science. Undergrads only, Grads use ARCH 5116. Learn how to decipher and deploy the subliminal conversations between humans and architecture through the art and science of Human-Centric Design (HCD). This course has three divisions: 1) How the Conversation Evolved – Evolution, History, Architects, Artists, Theories, and Cultures; 2) Human Communication Channels – Biology for Architects with scientific research and methods; and 3) Striking and Managing a Good Conversation – Application in Practice. Journal and sketch entries will be an integral part of this course and will challenge, develop, and analyze your current design process.

comments: Light Refractions: The atmospheric roles of light in design. Undergrads only, Grads use ARCH 5036. Light Refractions explores light as both an artistic and atmospheric element of design. The course expands the current proposition that “Architecture is Atmosphere” as presented by Elisabetta Canepa and Peter Zumthor, and as demonstrated through the works of Steven Holl, Tadao Ando and others. As a complement to architectural discourse, the experience of light is explored through the art of James Carpenter and James Turrell, and with invited guest, light artist Phillip Smith III. This class explores the interrelationships of light, space and perception that are the foundation to the embodied experience of architecture. The course also discusses the psychological and physiological impacts of light, particularly daylight, on occupant health and wellbeing.

subject: ARCH
title: Adv Env Controls
comments: Light Refractions: The atmospheric roles of light in design. Grads only, Undergrads use 4224. Light Refractions explores light as both an artistic and atmospheric element of design. The course expands the current proposition that “Architecture is Atmosphere” as presented by Elisabetta Canepa and Peter Zumthor, and as demonstrated through the works of Steven Holl, Tadao Ando and others. As a complement to architectural discourse, the experience of light is explored through the art of James Carpenter and James Turrell, and with invited guest, light artist Phillip Smith III. This class explores the interrelationships of light, space and perception that are the foundation to the embodied experience of architecture. The course also discusses the psychological and physiological impacts of light, particularly daylight, on occupant health and wellbeing.

subject: ARCH
title: Topics in Comp Appl Design
comments: Digital Modeling & Post-pro. Grads only, Undergrads use 3504. This course is an exciting blend of Rhinoceros for conceptual design, and Adobe Photoshop for post-production—giving you a well-rounded skill set to create and enhance stunning digital designs. You’ll start by mastering 2D drafting and progress to designing intricate 3D models using Rhinoceros, building a strong foundation in precision modeling. Then, in the post-production phase, we’ll dive into Photoshop’s advanced effects and visual techniques to polish your visuals with professional flair. Whether you’re new to these tools or looking to sharpen your skills, this course is designed to help you unlock your creative potential!

subject: ARCH
title: Topics in Comp Appl Design
comments: Immersive Design (VR +AI). Grads only, Undergrads use 3504. This course explores the rapidly evolving convergence of artificial intelligence (AI), virtual reality (VR), real-time rendering, and animation in design visualization. Students will gain hands-on experience with industry-leading platforms—Enscape, Twinmotion, and D5—while learning how to integrate AI-driven ideation and creativity tools into their design and storytelling workflows. The course Explores techniques for rendering, animation, and immersive VR experiences. Each platform will be presented not just as a visualization tool, but as a gateway to designing, animating, and experiencing projects in VR. Through these stages, students will explore the intersection of creativity, technical mastery, and narrative design—using AI to amplify imagination, animation to craft compelling stories, and VR to immerse audiences in bold new realities. Whether you’re new to these tools or looking to sharpen your skills, this course is designed to help you unlock your creative potential!

subject: ARCH
title: Topics in Comp Appl Design
comments: In this course in acoustic experiences and acoustic environments, students will learn about the role of acoustics in enhancing the quality of human life and well-being through physical and virtual environments. Acoustics is the science that deals with sound, and aural experiences deal with understanding the human perception of sound in different environments considering human cognition and the role of cultural background in sound perception. This is a project-based course in which the students will work in teams to analyze the aural experience of selected acoustic environments and design a physical or virtual aural experience that aims to enhance positive emotions, productivity, creativity, or a sense of community. The students will connect their learning to the real world by engaging with the community and participating in class discussions to reflect on their experiences. The evaluations and discussion will build a foundation for designing acoustic experience project.

subject: ARCH
title: Topics in Comp Appl Design
comments: Energy & Daylight Building Simulation. Graduates only. Undergrads use ARCH 3404. Achieving the optimal design isn't always guaranteed by good intentions alone. Sometimes, relying solely on intuition and general guidelines falls short in making well-informed decisions. This course is designed to introduce students to the use of several advanced building simulation tools, including the COVE tool (Energy Simulation), Grasshopper (Climate Report), and Climate Studio (Daylight simulation). The course will fill the gap between qualitative and quantitative aspects of design, considering the user experience in the daylight simulation stage. The primary focus is on designing and optimizing sustainable building systems through energy modeling in the early design stages to reduce environmental impact and enhance energy efficiency. Students will gain an understanding of the natural forces and human comfort factors that drive sustainable systems, as well as the various systems and cycles of our planet, including energy, atmosphere, and climate. No prior experience is required, and all licenses will be provided.

subject: ARCH
title: Topics in Comp Appl Design
comments: Com Design & Fabrication. Grads only, Undergrads use ARCH 3504. The Integrated Computational Design & Fabrication (ICDF) course introduces students to the intersection of computational design and digital fabrication in architecture. Students will gain hands-on experience with Grasshopper 3D, learning to design free-form objects/structures and create prototypes using advanced digital fabrication tools like Robotic Arm, CNC machines, and 3D printers. Through weekly modeling assignments and group projects, students will design and prototype an installation, integrating computational thinking with practical fabrication techniques. In the last month, we will make one of the projects on a real scale. The course aims to familiarize students with digital tools and processes, highlighting how fabrication capabilities influence architectural design and construction.

subject: ARCH
title: Topics in Comp Appl Design
comments: Architectural BIM (Revit). Grads only, Undergrads use ARCH 3504. This course introduces you to the core concepts and tools of Building Information Modeling (BIM) using Autodesk Revit. You'll gain the skills to create, analyze, and present architectural designs in both technical and visually compelling ways. Each week, we’ll explore key topics in detail, with clear explanations and hands-on exercises to help you really understand the material. As you progress, you’ll have the opportunity to apply your skills in more complex projects, building your confidence and expertise along the way. Whether you’re new to these tools or looking to sharpen your skills, this course is designed to help you unlock your creative potential!

subject: ARCH
title: Topics in Comp Appl Design
comments: Building the Future of Construction. Grads only, Undergrads use ARCH 3404. As part of the CDR OpenLab and through this project-based collaboration with the National Building Museum (NBM), the Center for Design Research(CDR) course will envision “the air and space museum for construction” through the development of experiential exhibitions that address cycles of innovation in construction’s past, present, and future and engage stakeholders across disciplines, ages, and backgrounds. During the course students will explore the museum as a place of culture and learning while experimenting with technologies such as XR and spatial computing. Course is open to all disciplines and levels and will include travel to Washington DC for an NBM visit.

subject: ARCH
title: Media & Environment
comments: Virtual Travel Sketching. Grads only, Undergrads use ARCH 3504. As an initial response to the limitations on travel during the pandemic, this elective course was developed in 2020 to allow students to engage in travel study through drawing without traveling physically. Using digital means, we “traveled” to 15 locations across the world and worked through a series of drawing exercises that equipped students with the habits and ways of thinking through drawing—to see, study, and analyze their future physical travel experiences as architects. The review of drawings on screen via zoom worked surprisingly well with greater ability to engage with the “tactics” and decision process of making a drawing enabling direct discussion, critique, and demonstration from both the instructor and student colleagues. In Spring of 2026, this course returns as a hybrid course designed to focus your understanding of sketching practices as an architect. Emphasis will be on formulating “the page” as a drawing problem. How do you plan a series of drawings with an intention; making drawings that are exploratory and analytic, working to build pages in a sketchbook that (foster?) an understanding of what you see rather than simply “taking a pic.” Various approaches to drawing are explored and experiment will be encouraged.

subject: ARCH
title: Media & Environment
comments: TS: Unreal Engine for Arch. Graduates only. Undergraduates please use ARCH 3504. Check computer requirements before enrolling in this course. This course introduces architecture students to the capabilities of Unreal Engine 5 for architectural visualization. Students will learn how to create immersive environments, render high-quality images, cinematics, and be introduced to blueprint coding language. Through a blend of technical tutorials and projects, students will explore lighting, materials, and real-time rendering techniques.

subject: ARCH
title: Media & Environment
comments: Material Design: From Nanoscale Building Blocks to Macroscale Structures. Graduates only. Undergraduates please use ARCH 3404. In this course, we examine the interplay between man-made and natural materials. We will investigate how nano properties influence macro scale applications, with a focus on synthetic, bioinspired, and biomaterials. Students will design, fabricate, and test their own materials, bridging theoretical concepts with practical applications. We will explore both traditional material engineering and bioengineering approaches, assessing how biological principles inform sustainable design. Students will analyze and characterize their creations using cutting-edge methods in material science, such as Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), Nanoindentation, and Universal Testing Machine (UTM). By the end of the course, students will be equipped with a critical, creative mindset for material specification in architectural design and construction. This course is designed to make complex material science accessible, with no prior knowledge required, and will inspire students to explore new possibilities in architecture, from the molecular scale to the building scale Join us as we explore new worlds from nano to macro!"

subject: ARCH
title: Media & Environment
comments: TS: Mapping the Built. Graduates only. Undergrads please use ARCH 3504. Introduction to science and art of cartography, including the conceptual framework of the cartographic method. Development of the skills necessary to create maps to be used in the reading, analysis, and interpretation of spatial arrangements, with an emphasis on data collection, evaluation, and synthesis using applicable technologies such as Geographic Information Systems (GIS). Analysis and synthesis of results will be explored that consider the impact of using platform technologies at varying scales in the planning and design process, on the built environment.

subject: ARCH
title: Media & Environment

subject: ARCH
title: Media & Environment
comments: Human-Centric Design: The Art and Science. Grads only, Undergrads use ARCH 3604. Learn how to decipher and deploy the subliminal conversations between humans and architecture through the art and science of Human-Centric Design (HCD). This course has three divisions: 1) How the Conversation Evolved – Evolution, History, Architects, Artists, Theories, and Cultures; 2) Human Communication Channels – Biology for Architects with scientific research and methods; and 3) Striking and Managing a Good Conversation – Application in Practice. Journal and sketch entries will be an integral part of this course and will challenge, develop, and analyze your current design process.

subject: ARCH
title: Top Arch Hist Theory
comments: Blind Design Workshop. Grads only, Undergrads use ARCH 3234 In the spring of 2026, a group of learners who are blind or visually-impaired, organized by the Virginia Department for the Blind and Vision Impaired (DBVI), will participate in an immersive design workshop at Virginia Tech which will be led by faculty and students of the Schools of Architecture + Design. The workshop will engage participants with a blind-accessible design project, supplemented by guest lectures, videos + readings, tours of sites in and around the university, and instruction in emerging building technologies. It will provide career exploration experience in the discipline of architecture, and give participants the opportunity to improve their self-advocacy skills while interacting with university students and navigating a college campus. Virginia Tech students, working under the guidance of Dr. Andrew Gipe-Lazarou, will receive university credit for preparing and instructing the workshop, which will both address the spatial needs of the blind community and call into question the ‘ocular-centrism’ of design by exploring ways in which architecture can be instructed non-visually. Workshop preparation will be supplemented by a hands-on tutorial organized by DBVI about working / interacting with individuals who are blind or visually impaired.

subject: ASPT
title: TS: Env Thry & Politcs Plnt
comments: Environmental Theory and Politics in the Plantationocene The rise of Indigenous, peasant, and poor peoples’ environmental movements in recent decades have reshaped environmental politics and raised important questions for conceptualizing the present and alternatives in a moment of ecological and political peril. These movements have posited concepts buen vivir, body-territory, autonomy, and food and land sovereignty as paradigmatic challenges to dominant paradigms of development and modernity while building heterogeneous alliances within and across borders. This course examines these movements and their potential through theoretical and ethnographic accounts. Readings will explore shifting patterns of capital accumulation and resource exploitation; movements in defense of water of territory against extractive industries; agrarian struggles and critiques of plantation ecologies; alliance building; convergences and divergences with anti-colonial nationalist political horizons; and patterns of criminalization and repression. What commitments, solidarities, and ontologies motivate these movements? What are their strategies and tactics? How have the conditions of possibility for these movements shifted through neoliberalism to the present? Are theories of Plantationocene, the Pluriverse, decolonization, and degrowth capacious and coherent enough to harness affinities between diverse movements? What is their potential to challenge eco-colonialism and authoritarian imperialism?

subject: CS
title: Computer Science Capstone
comments: AI, Learning & Education — Explore how computational systems can reduce the negative impacts of AI on learning while creating productive new ways for students and instructors to work with AI. Teams will identify a real-world problem and design and build a solution focused on areas such as AI literacy, critical engagement, learning, or instructor support. For information on capstone topics: https://students.cs.vt.edu/undergraduate-programs/current-students/Capstones.html

subject: CS
title: Computer Science Capstone
comments: Computational Science — Work in a team on a computationally intensive research project involving areas such as numerical methods, algorithms, HPC, GPUs, advanced software, and visualization. This option provides experience with the full lifecycle of a computation-heavy R&D project and is also good preparation for graduate study. For information on capstone topics: https://students.cs.vt.edu/undergraduate-programs/current-students/Capstones.html

subject: CS
title: Computer Science Capstone
comments: Educational Technology — Design, build, and evaluate educational technology using PrairieLearn, an open-source learning and assessment platform, while applying ideas from software engineering, learning science, and AI. Projects may include AI tutoring, AI-assisted feedback and grading, question-authoring tools, interactive assessments, or instructor analytics. For information on capstone topics: https://students.cs.vt.edu/undergraduate-programs/current-students/Capstones.html

subject: CS
title: Computer Science Capstone
comments: Computational Biology — Combine computing, biological data, and mathematical or computational modeling to investigate a biological system or research question. Teams will conduct collaborative research on topics such as gene regulation, infectious disease, population dynamics, signaling pathways, or systems biology. For information on capstone topics: https://students.cs.vt.edu/undergraduate-programs/current-students/Capstones.html

subject: CS
title: Computer Science Capstone
comments: Real-World Software Development — Work with an external client to design, develop, test, and prepare a functional software application for deployment. Teams will gain experience with software development, project management, teamwork, and the responsible use of AI throughout the development process. For information on capstone topics: https://students.cs.vt.edu/undergraduate-programs/current-students/Capstones.html

subject: CS
title: Computer Science Capstone
comments: Social Computing — Explore how technology can help people communicate, collaborate, learn, and make decisions together. Teams will design and build a solution to a real social or collaborative problem, with possibilities including AI-supported teamwork, collaborative learning, online communities, group discussions, and human-AI collaboration. For information on capstone topics: https://students.cs.vt.edu/undergraduate-programs/current-students/Capstones.html

subject: ECE
title: SS: CMOS-Micro/Nano Systems
comments: A-F only. The audit option is not available. This course accepts force-add requests from students in other degree programs. Fill out the undergrad force-add form survey found at https://ece.vt.edu/undergrad/policies.html COURSE DESCRIPTION: This course introduces the principles, design methodologies, and applications of CMOS-based micro/nano systems for sensing, computation, and bio-interfacing. Topics include CMOS front-end design, analog-to-digital converters, micro/nano electrode arrays, electrode characterization, and hybrid CMOS–nano integration for high-throughput bio/medical applications. Students will also explore concepts of neuromorphic chip design and neural interfaces bridging natural and artificial intelligence. Emphasis is placed on system-level thinking, critical evaluation of emerging research, and design projects addressing real-world challenges in healthcare, neuroscience, and artificial intelligence.

title: SS: CMOS-Micro/Nano Systems
comments: A-F only. The audit option is not available. This course accepts force-add requests from students in other degree programs. Access the Force-Add forms through this link: https://ece.vt.edu/grad/forms COURSE DESCRIPTION: This course introduces the principles, design methodologies, and applications of CMOS-based micro/nano systems for sensing, computation, and bio-interfacing. Topics include CMOS front-end design, analog-to-digital converters, micro/nano electrode arrays, electrode characterization, and hybrid CMOS–nano integration for high-throughput bio/medical applications. Emphasis is placed on system-level thinking, critical evaluation of emerging research, and design projects addressing real-world challenges in healthcare, neuroscience, and artificial intelligence.

subject: ECE
title: SS: Power Device Characteriz
comments: A-F only. The Audit option is NOT available. COURSE DESCRIPTION. Hands-on, lab-based course covering techniques and best practices for wide-band-gap (WBG) device characterization, driving, and protection. Students conduct experimental static and dynamic testing of WBG devices, developing models of experimental performance. Characterization results support advanced modeling, design, and optimization of power converters leveraging WBG devices. Course content includes static characterization using a high power curve tracer; modeling and simulating device switching behavior; and designing, constructing, and debugging a double-pulse-test circuit board for dynamic characterization. (2H, 3L, 3C)

subject: ECE
title: SS: Optical Sensing & Imaging
comments: A-F only. The Audit option is NOT available. This course accepts force-add requests from students in other degree programs only with the instructor's permission. COURSE DESCRIPTION. This course provides a comprehensive overview of the fundamental principles and selected techniques of optical sensing and imaging, as well as modern simulation tools. It covers light propagation, image formation, resolution, interferometry, spectroscopy, and light-matter interaction, with applications to modern sensing and imaging systems. Topics include conventional and computational imaging, spectral and white-light interferometry, optical coherence tomography, fiber-optic and distributed sensing, fluorescence-based methods, Raman spectroscopy, and selected advanced microscopy techniques, emphasizing operating principles, system implementation, performance metrics, and applications.

subject: ECON
title: TS: ECON Data-Driven Decisions
comments: This is a course built around the perspective of the decision-makers (e.g., managers, executives, stakeholders), which is valuable for analysts who support the decision-making, as well as those with such responsibilities. Fundamentally, this course is designed with the belief that humans are ultimately responsible for decision-making which leads to actions and outcomes. The human comparative advantage in data-driven decision-making lies in intuition, context, and ethical judgment. While machines can process and analyze vast amounts of data efficiently, humans excel at interpreting complex, ambiguous situations and applying broader context and experience. Humans also bring creativity, emotional intelligence, and moral reasoning into decisions: qualities that machines cannot replicate. Prerequisites: ECON 2005, 2006, and Sophomore standing or above.

subject: ECON
title: TS: DC Experience in ECON
comments: An experiential blended learning course that showcases the ecosystem of startups economics, policy and associated policy environment. Prepare for the race to the future using the principles of strategic planning at the world's best and fast-growing startup destinations. Become equipped with the playbook to generate startup ideas from insights, trends, talks, and panels. Learn to navigate the detours to create or work for a successful startup. Gain insight into the art (storytelling) and science (data) of pitching ideas and gaining traction. Develop a professional network through corporate visits, startup presentations, meetings and conferences. The course requires a travel component to Austin, Texas to attend SXSW and additional meeting times outside of the schedule class time. Students are both financially and logistically responsibility for arranging this travel during the first few weeks of the semester. Students must acknowledge this travel component and request enrollment at https://forms.gle/ULQpPoMBz9xz3gAd7. Students will be manually enrolled in the order that they sign up. Once the course reaches capacity, additional students will be wait-listed.

subject: ECON
title: TS: ECON of Consulting-UG
comments: A comprehensive introduction to the field of Economic Consulting with a specialized focus on Financial Risk Consulting. This course equips students with the tools and methodologies required to address complex financial challenges faced by businesses today. Students will gain a solid foundation in economic and financial principles while developing the analytical skills necessary for effective risk assessment and mitigation. Topics covered include risk identification, quantification, and management, with an emphasis on credit, market, operational, and liquidity risk. The course integrates theoretical insights with practical applications, using case studies, data analysis, and real-world scenarios to enhance students' problem-solving abilities. Upon completion, students will be able to provide insightful financial consulting services, identify and analyze risks in diverse financial contexts, and offer strategic recommendations for risk mitigation and decision-making. Pre-Reqs: ECON 3254 or 4304.

subject: ECON
title: TS: Quant Finance
comments: This applied data science course provides a broad overview of modern quantitative Finance, across asset management, banking and insurance. It will covers the theoretical, computational and mathematical underpinnings of the advanced quantitative techniques in machine learning, econometrics, risk and portfolio management, algorithmic trading and Financial forecasting. At the end of the course, students will be able to implement the techniques themselves in Python. The course will provide a gentle introduction to programming using Python in the class. Pre-Reqs: ECON 3254 or ECON 4304 or CMDA 3654 or STAT 3006

subject: HIST
title: Crit Reading/Analysis in Hist
comments: Topic: Interpreting the Sixties. This course will examine how historians have interpreted the significance of the 1960s in America society, politics and culture. Focusing on writings about student movements, presidential politics, and popular culture, the class will explore how historical knowledge is produced and interpreted as part of an evolving scholarly conversation. In the process, students will hone their skills in critical reading, writing, and analysis.

subject: HIST
title: History Research Seminar
comments: TS: Long Civil War and Greater Reconstruction. Expanding the chronology and geography of the American Civil War, this capstone research will engage recent trends in scholarship on the “Long Civil War Era” and “Greater Reconstruction.” Looking beyond Appomattox, this includes alternative vantage points in broader conflicts over slavery and Free Soil; westward expansion and Indigenous resistance; reconstructions, reconciliation, and memory.

subject: HIST
title: History Research Seminar
comments: The wave of revolutionary uprisings in the Arab world in 2011 were a surprise to many. Experts had long been aware of deep political, social, and economic problems in the region. This research seminar will interrogate democracy, authoritarianism, and Islamism from a historical perspective. We will discuss the changing role of minorities, youth, and women in the public sphere. Asking questions like: what conditions lead to revolution? How are mass publics created and heard? And what role have authoritarian leaders and neoliberal policies played in provoking and squelching mass protests? Drawing on themes presented in class, students will complete a research paper on a related topic of their choice.

subject: HIST
title: Res Methods for Historians
comments: Building from HIST 5104: Historical Methods, Research Methods focuses on the mechanics of historical research and writing. It targets skills needed for the thesis writing process in a context that allows students to focus directly on their interests and allows for interdisciplinary dialogue. Assignments will target the specific components of conceptualizing, drafting, and completing a major piece of orginial research and culminate in a research proposal suitable for completing the MA research requirement (thesis or research paper). subject: ME
title: SS: Intro Comp Fluid Dynamics
comments: ME 3414 is a prerequisite Course description: This advanced undergraduate course introduces the theory and application of computational fluid dynamics (CFD), focusing on the solution of fluid flow problems using both commercial CFD software (ANSYS Fluent) and basic coding in Python or MATLAB. Students will develop foundational understanding of numerical methods and modeling principles while completing weekly hands-on labs with simulation assignments.

subject: ME
title: SS: Modern AI Tools for MechEs
comments: Introduction to using modern AI tools such as LLM chatbots and agentic AI for mechanical engineering. Basics of AI will be introduced and hands on training of how to use AI tools for engineering tasks such as design, optimization, and data analysis. Broader impacts, challenges, and opportunities presented by AI on engineering as a profession and society as a whole will be examined along with ethical use of AI

title: Knowledge and Reality
comments: Are your thoughts inside of your brain? Can you ever be completely certain of anything? Is it possible to travel back in time? Why is there evil in the world? Are values always subjective? In this course, you will explore these and other questions and learn how to debate them in a philosophically rigorous way.

subject: PHIL
title: Morality and Justice
comments: This course is an introduction to ethics, in which we aspire to get a better understanding of right and wrong action. We begin by investigating various ethical problems (e.g., abortion, global poverty, and genetic enhancement). We then discuss some theories of right and wrong action. Lastly, we investigate the nature and origins of right and wrong action more generally.

title: Morality and Justice
comments: This course provides an introduction to the major traditions in Western moral philosophy. Readings from Plato, Aristotle, David Hume, Immanuel Kant, and John Stuart Mill, sandwiched between two works of literature by Bertolt Brecht and Kurt Vonnegut.

subject: PHIL
title: Critical Thinking
comments: We'll study how to think about whether you have good reason to believe something, i.e., how to reconstruct and evaluate arguments for a position. First, we'll look at how to evaluate under "ideal" conditions, when you know perfectly well how an argument is supposed to go. Then we'll look at the normal, messy cases, and learn how to reconstruct arguments from incomplete and unclear starting points.

subject: PHIL
title: History of Modern Philosophy
comments: Late 18th and 19th century philosophy. We will begin with the challenge posed to epistemology by classic skeptical arguments, the most prominent being Cartesian rationalist skepticism and Humean empiricist skepticism. We move on to analyze the responses to skepticism by idealists and naturalists. In the second part of the course, we will trace the landmark influence of positivist philosophers on politics, on sociology, and on political thought, including the formation of governments.

subject: PHIL
title: Global Ethics
comments: This course examines urgent moral issues in the lives of 21st-century young adults. What does it mean to be a global citizen? Why do so many have so little? How do we stem the tide of imperialism, oppression, and neocolonial violence? What will the world look like in 20 years, 50, or 100? This class is discussion-based and makes heavy use of movies, shows, and social media, in addition to books and papers.

subject: PHIL
title: Global Ethics
comments: Students are asked to think critically about what it means to live an ethical life in a global context, within the larger structures that govern our lives. To that end, we critically evaluate philosophical arguments that apply ethical principles to such contemporary global issues as climate change, global poverty, foreign aid, international immigration, and economic justice. The course's central goal is to encourage students to develop well-reasoned and well-supported viewpoints on contemporary global ethical challenges.

subject: PHIL
title: TS: Copyright Law and AI
comments: This course inquires into how copyright law addresses technological change with a focus on generative artificial intelligence. We begin by looking at the philosophical foundations of copyright. Then we examine the constitutional and statutory structure of U.S. copyright law, gaining familiarity with the central copyright rules, principles, and doctrines by reading several judicial decisions. From there, we review some historical examples of how American copyright law adapted to accommodate technological change. Finally, we consider current issues, concerns, case law, and debates about how copyright law should respond to generative AI.

subject: PHIL
title: Biomedical Ethics
comments: This course will provide students with the opportunity to critically reflect on important issues within contemporary biomedical ethics, while developing skills in philosophical debate and argument analysis. Topics will include dilemmas from the beginnings to the end of life, covering ethical debates on issues such as embryo research, assisted reproductive technology, genetic selection, abortion, and assisted dying. Students will have the opportunity to select topics for consideration. Classes are discussion-based, and a high level of active participation is required.

title: Modern Logic & Dev
comments: Broadly speaking, logic is the study of correct reasoning. This class provides a general introduction to formal symbolic logic. We will cover the syntax and semantics of sentential and predicate logic, as well as a derivation system for each.

subject: PHIL
title: TS: Phil Decision Theory
comments: All students welcome. Pathways approved. Course Information: Classical decision theory is a mathematical framework for modeling action under conditions of uncertainty. It has been highly influential across a wide range of fields, including economics, political science, philosophy, psychology, and sociology. This course will introduce the theory and examine a range of philosophical puzzles it raises, with the aim of developing a deeper understanding of its foundations.

subject: PHIL
title: Special Topics in Philosophy
comments: This course provides an overview of continental philosophy, tracing major developments in 19th and 20th century French and German thought. We will examine the influence and contemporary relevance of Marxism, transcendental and existential phenomenology, and their critical reworking by later twentieth-century thinkers. Alongside close readings of foundational texts in continental philosophy, the course will explore how these traditions can inform contemporary critiques of colonialism, racism, gender subordination, and heterosexism.

subject: PHIL
title: Epistemology
comments: We'll investigate what it means to have good reason to believe a proposition and the difference between mere justified belief and knowledge. We'll examine theories of how justification works. We'll also pay special attention to whether it's possible to have any kind of justified belief in ordinary propositions, even when granted the possibility of knowledge about things that are happening right in front of you, right now.

subject: PHIL
title: Special Topics in Philosophy
comments: The focus of this seminar is grounding, a notion that has played an important role in metaphysics over the past fifteen years or so. Central questions include: How does grounding relate to fundamentality? To causation and causal explanation? What theoretical work might we put the notion to? Are there reasons to be skeptical of grounding?

subject: PHIL
title: Special Topics in Philosophy
comments: This course will introduce classical decision theory and examine a range of philosophical puzzles raised by the theory. The first half of the course will focus on developing fluency with the mathematical theory. The second half of the course will focus on various philosophical puzzles associated with the theory, along with contemporary discussions of those puzzles.

subject: PHS
title: Undergraduate Research
comments: TEAM Malawi [Technology-Education-Advocacy-Medicine] is a transdisciplinary collaboration, based upon a community wellness model of health, designed to meet the challenges of resource-limited environments through community based participatory research/design/teaching.  Vision: Utilize a community wellness model as the framework to integrate the activities of a disparate group of young investigators and mentors.  Primary Goal: Student Engagement, and it is our desire to:  Foster global perspectives of students.  Stimulate ideas for improving conditions in a developing country.  Create sustainable relationships that promote transdisciplinary models for development.  Encourage evidence-based applied scholarly research.

comments: Modeling the Mind: Linking Cognitive Processes and Brain Data. By the end of the course, students will be able to critically evaluate methodological choices in the literature, plan their own analysis pipelines, and interpret findings in the context of high-level theoretical questions about how the brain learns and makes decisions. This course is designed for graduate students in psychology, neuroscience, engineering, or related fields who want to deepen their understanding of human neuroimaging and computational approaches to cognition, especially in learning and decision making. Prior experience with neuroimaging data is not required—only curiosity and a willingness to engage with the material.

subject: SOC
title: Intro Data in Social Context
comments: Focus on contemporary uses of data in medicine, science, and algorithms. Counts towards the Complementary Skills requirement for History Majors, but cannot count towards both Complementary Skills and CLE or Pathways. Introduction to Data in Social Context examines data as a plural category with a focus on their social and political implications. Supported by empirical literature, this course sheds light on the inherently social nature of producing, collecting, processing, analyzing, and applying data, especially in view of increasingly pervasive predictive policies. It emphasizes the cultural aspects in which any kind of data is embedded, to leverage students’ critical understanding of the role of individuals, private and public institutions in perpetuating social inequalities and unfair relations through decision-making processes. Throughout the semester, students will address the question “what can go wrong” when working with data in a variety of contexts, considering questions related to ableism, class, ethnicity, gender, race, and the global South. The course interrogates notions of objectivity and subjectivity in data and decisions, and challenges students to imagine futures where social justice values are at the core of data and decisions.
